In Study~2, GPT-5.3-codex achieves the highest resolution rate in this sample (81.2\%), ahead of Claude Opus~4.6 (68.9\%) and GPT-4.1-mini (25.0\%), but resolved-task-normalized efficiency remains mixed: GPT-4.1-mini is lowest on estimated carbon and cost per resolved task, while GPT-5.3-codex delivers substantially higher task success. All carbon estimates cover output-token inference only; prompt tokens, which exceed 99\% of tokens in Study~2, and tool execution are not charged, so the figures are lower bounds on the full agentic footprint.

title: Embodied First Exam
authors: Kangrui Wang and Qineng Wang and Changhe Chen and Pingyue Zhang and Chi Gui and Feishi Wang and Canyu Chen and Wenli Xiao and Xiaoyu Huang and Tonghe Zhang and Linjie Li and Zihan Wang and Minyeong Kim and Yiyou Sun and Mingkai Deng and Jinyu Hou and Qi Zhu and Han Liu and Eric P. Xing and Huaxiu Yao and Zhiwen Fan and Yuejiang Liu and Dawn Song and Pieter Abbeel and Li Fei-Fei and Jiajun Wu and Yuke Zhu and Guanya Shi and Ruohan Zhang and Manling Li
abstract: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.

title: Unmasking shortcut solutions of coding agents on partial differential equations
authors: Jiale Linghu and Yangshuai Wang
abstract: Coding agents now write simulation programs, but benchmarks usually judge only whether their output matches a reference. In manufactured-solution tasks the data determine the exact solution, so a matching output need not come from a solver. We introduce PDEViBench, a benchmark of 290 tasks in six equation families that traces each passing program to the computation behind its output and reruns unclear programs on changed data. A Codex agent (GPT-5.2) passed 80% of 1,450 runs, yet about one pass in ten returned the exact solution without solving the equation. Counting only solved passes changed which task features made problems seem hard and reversed the ranking of two prompts. Once the prompt forbade the shortcut, every pass was a numerical solve, and on tasks without a closed-form solution passing programs stayed correct on changed data. Scientific coding benchmarks should check how each answer was computed as well as whether it matches.

title: SHADOWPREFILL: Keeping Your Next Model Warm for Per-Step Model Routing in Agentic LLM Serving
authors: Haoran Qiu and Rohan Mahapatra and Rodrigo Fonseca and Mark Russinovich
abstract: Per-step model routers send each LLM call of an agent to the cost-optimal model dynamically within each session. However, every model switch discards prefix-cache reuse: KV caches are per model, so the new model must prefill the relevant context before it emits a token. Across representative agentic workloads, including a production coding-agent trace with a mean context of 63K tokens, the prefix hit rate falls from 80-89% on same model calls to 44-65% after a switch, and a switch call takes 1.5-3.2x as long. We present SHADOWPREFILL, which prefills the session's context on the model the router has not chosen, in capacity that instances serving normal traffic leave idle, so the next switch finds its prefix cached. SHADOWPREFILL harvests the per-iteration SLO slack of requests in flight, protects routed calls, spills shadow KV to host memory, and falls back to a cold switch whenever the shadow is incomplete. With LLMRouter routing 24 model pairs over five agentic benchmark suites, SHADOWPREFILL cuts switch-call latency by 8.5-21.4%, LLM-call latency by 3.7-17.7%, and routed token cost by 22.5-46.1%, while normal traffic keeps its SLO and energy per request rises by 0.4%.

title: FlowPlan: Reducing the Token Cost of Coding Agents with Abstraction-Guided Planning and Verification
authors: Melika Sepidband and Jiho Shin and Song Wang and Hadi Hemmati
abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code can resolve real-world repository issues, but their iterative interaction loop can be expensive. Existing approaches reduce this cost primarily by limiting, compressing, or selectively avoiding information and actions within the repair process. We investigate a complementary question: Can an agent reason about a repair at an abstract program level, rather than repeatedly operating over raw source code, to reduce both the exploration needed to identify a repair and the repeated checking needed to verify it afterward? We present FlowPlan, an abstraction-guided repair approach that structures localization, planning, and verification around per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs. The agent first localizes the candidate fault location on the program abstraction and expresses the intended repair as explicit graph deltas before modifying the concrete source. After the edit, FlowPlan reconstructs the same abstraction and compares the observed structural change with the planned one. Then, a verification checks the complete repair before termination. Across all six benchmark-model settings, FlowPlan does not significantly change resolution rate relative to the vanilla agent while reducing token consumption in every setting, significantly in five of six settings. With Claude Haiku 4.5, it uses only 0.46-0.47x the baseline tokens on SWE-bench Pro, 0.32-0.35x on SWE-bench Verified, and 0.68-0.74x on SecBench; with Sonnet 5, it uses 0.72-0.76x, 0.73-0.74x, and 0.92-0.94x, respectively. Overall, FlowPlan achieves the largest token reduction among the compared methods in three of the six settings and ties the strongest compared method in a fourth. Trajectory analysis shows that FlowPlan saves tokens by replacing much of the costly post-edit re-reading and testing with explicit verification and reducing per-call context.

title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
authors: Josip Vrdoljak and Akash Singh and Bas Steunebrink and Alex Yarotsky and John Lorenzo and Achille Nicoletti and Sam Pigott
abstract: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.

title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
authors: Shyam Agarwal and Olga Lvova and Agnia Sergeyuk and Anastasiia Serova and Timofey Bryksin and Thomas Zimmermann and Bogdan Vasilescu
abstract: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.

title: Scaling Shapley Energy Attribution to Large LLM Batches
authors: Qi Luo and Ziwen Wang and Kunlin Li and Changxi Liu and Yun Chen
abstract: LLM services have become essential infrastructure for applications such as chat assistants and coding agents. Service providers need to attribute resource consumption to individual requests for purposes such as billing. Among these resources, energy is a key metric for assessing the cost of serving each request. However, serving engines batch requests together, and GPUs report only aggregate energy consumption. Providers typically estimate each request's share in proportion to its token consumption, but this approach can produce substantially unfair estimates. The Shapley value provides a principled solution to fair energy allocation, but computing it directly requires $2^N-1$ GPU runs for $N$ requests, which is infeasible for large batches. To address this problem, we propose StepSplit. Across GPU generations, we observe that the energy consumed by each inference step, a forward pass over a batch, consists of a shared energy, largely due to reading model weights, and a request-specific energy. We derive a closed-form Shapley value: each request is charged its own energy plus an equal part of the shared energy of every step in which it participates. A microbenchmark of 2.5-17.8 minutes calibrates both parts of the step energy once per model and GPU configuration. Under static batching, StepSplit uses this closed form in a single pass over the scheduler log. Under continuous batching, removing a request can change how the remaining requests are batched, so StepSplit adds a correction to the closed form, computed by replaying the scheduler on a CPU. We evaluate StepSplit against Shapley values measured using 529,513 GPU runs. Under static batching with batch sizes of 8-256, StepSplit achieves an $L_1$ error of 0.4-4.3%, compared with 13.4-61.3% for token-proportional allocation. Under continuous batching with 8-128 requests, the corresponding errors are 0.5-6.4% and 20.6-71.7%.

title: BioXArena-Pro: a research-grade benchmark for autonomous biomedical machine learning agents
authors: Loka Li and Duzhen Zhang and Xingbo Du and Leonard Song and Kun Zhang and Le Song
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous builders of biomedical models, but existing benchmarks are small, near saturation or open to leaked information. We present BioXArena-Pro, 64 research-level modelling tasks from eight biomedical domains, each rebuilt from a published study; most hold out whole biological units such as species or cohorts. Across 22 agent configurations, the best scores 55.1 of 100, and the scaffold matters almost as much as the model. We re-ran a published method for every task: where the published recipe applies unchanged, the best agent and the methods tie; on rebuilt tasks the methods trail by 8.2 points, suggesting that agents gain by adapting to new data. Pretrained models (including biological foundation models) matter where the strongest agent uses them: forbidding them decreases its score on those tasks by 9 points. Every task was audited in several AI-assisted rounds and a final human review.

title: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
authors: Lirui Luo and Kelong Mao and Xinwei Yang and Rongqing Li and Luyu Chen and Kieran Wong and Yudong Guo and Xinrui Wang and Jiayin Zhu and Pu Yao and Gu Simiu and Sulong Xu and Cong Fang
abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
authors: Martim Afonso and Inês Lynce and Maurizio Morisio and João F. Ferreira
abstract: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. On the best-performing configurations, ProofCoder increases proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-theart AutoRocq system, corresponding to a 27.7% relative improvement at approximately half the cost. Our ablations identify continuous reasoning as a key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies. These results suggest that effective automated software verification requires more than improved tactic selection: continuous reasoning and feedback-guided proof revision are critical ingredients for robust proof synthesis.

title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
authors: Zhengxiang Huang and Yujie Sun and Shengheng Chen and Zhaode Wang and Chaoyue Niu and Zeyu Zhao and Chengfei Lv and Fan Wu and Guihai Chen
abstract: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
authors: Ilia Larchenko and Gleb Zarin and Atindra Nair and Keerti Manney and Vitaly Kleban and Mirko Kiefer and Anjana Yodaiken
abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

title: JoyFrontBench: Evaluating Front-End Coding Agents through Goal-Oriented Acceptance Contracts
authors: Xiaoyi Qiao and Yicheng Wang and Jianan Lin and Xiaoyang Ji and Dongyi Lv and Yidan Huang and Shi Suo and Shiying Fan and Nan Duan and Jiaqi Wang
abstract: Front-end coding agents are expected to produce applications that fulfill user goals, yet high task scores can coexist with failures in essential workflows. Evaluating these agents therefore requires an explicit distinction between partial implementation and application success. We introduce JoyFrontBench, a benchmark that makes this distinction through goal-oriented acceptance contracts. Each contract identifies core tasks and mandatory criteria before generation: a core task passes only when all mandatory criteria are satisfied and a shared completion threshold is met, while application success requires every core task to pass on the same operational artifact within a single run. Derived from practitioner requirements, JoyFrontBench comprises 100 front-end development problems, 764 tasks, and 2,596 atomic criteria, with reviewed annotations linking user goals to core tasks and evidence requirements. The evaluation framework combines evidence-grounded judgments with deterministic record auditing and fixed scoring rules, preserving graded task assessment alongside explicit core-task and application-level acceptance. We evaluate five coding models under two agent harnesses, OpenHands and OpenCode, on the 70-problem test set; the remaining 30 problems form a public set for validation and diagnostic analyses. Under OpenHands, the mean Average Task Score (ATS) across models is 87.69%, while the mean Application Success Rate (ASR) is 51.52%. Further analyses reveal changes in model rankings across harnesses and variation in application success across repeated runs. These findings highlight the limitations of aggregate task scores in characterizing application success and motivate explicit assessment of core-goal fulfillment alongside graded task performance.

title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
authors: Jiayu Ding and Yupan Huang and Jinyoung Park and Yilin Jia and Wenshan Wu and Tengchao Lv and Shaohan Huang and Yuzhong Zhao and Xiangyang Zhou and Tao Ge and Sun Mao and Xun Wang and Huitian Jiao and Si-Qing Chen and Lei Cui and Nanning Zheng and Furu Wei
abstract: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
authors: Zhengyang Ai and Tong Liu and Jingxian Tang and Xiaobing Du and Tao Xiao and Fengshi Zhang and Zishuo Li and Xiaodong Ai and Pinyan Lu
abstract: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

title: Technical Debt Risks in AI-Assisted Software Development: Insights from Practitioners
authors: Nazia Jahan and Nafisa Alam and Sourov Debnath and Arafat Rahman and S. M. Waesh Ahmed and Md Farhad Alam Bhuiyan and Mia Mohammad Imran
abstract: AI coding assistants increasingly support software development, raising concerns about technical debt associated with AI-generated code and development practices. We investigate these concerns through a sequential mixed-methods study involving 137 survey respondents and 20 follow-up interviews with software professionals in Bangladesh. Drawing on ten established technical debt dimensions, we examine perceived risks, contributing circumstances, maintenance consequences, validation practices, and developer understanding. Respondents expressed the strongest concerns about People Debt (73.0\%), Management Debt (70.1\%), and Architecture Debt (68.6\%), suggesting that risks extend beyond code quality. Participants associated ambiguous requirements, insufficient project context, and unrequested AI-generated changes with architectural inconsistencies, rework, and maintenance difficulties. Their experiences revealed contrasting outcomes: AI assistance supported refactoring, maintainability improvements, and testing, but also introduced rework and context misalignment. Although 89.8\% reported regularly verifying AI-generated code, participants expressed concerns about AI dependence, reduced code understanding, and review effort. They also emphasized the need for stronger architectural awareness, requirements clarification, and validation support in coding assistants. Our findings suggest that managing technical debt risks requires attention to project context, implementation decisions, and developer understanding alongside generated code quality.

title: Bug Finding With Agentic Symbolic Execution
authors: George Granberry and Wolfgang Ahrendt and Andy Gordon and Moa Johansson
abstract: Symbolic execution, in tools such as CrossHair for Python, is a powerful technique for finding bugs, but two barriers hinder its adoption: the human effort of annotating code with assertions, and the need to model the execution environment outside Python, such as an external database. To overcome both, we design an agentic harness that orchestrates the symbolic execution tool CrossHair together with an AI coding agent. Without human intervention, it instruments a repository with assertions, synthesizes a constraint-aware symbolic environment for the database, runs symbolic execution, and constructs a concrete test as evidence for each bug it reports. We evaluate our harness on 1,156,044 lines of Python code over 11 popular open-source Python web applications (Zulip, NetBox, Apache Superset, and others). With the synthesized environment, CrossHair executes 81% of the 5,406 contracted functions, against 4.5% without it. Our pipeline finds 1,050 bugs, each reproduced by a test against the unmodified application, 221 of them by CrossHair, and 312 of them are missed by a baseline in which the same LLM inspects the code. The two find different kinds of bugs: CrossHair's are mostly crashes on input-domain corner cases that validation admits, such as empty strings, missing fields and unusual characters, while inspection's are mostly bugs that produce wrong output. Our framework thus lets symbolic execution supplement inspection-based bug finding.

title: What World Model Does Active Object Search Need? A Study under Imperfect Detection
authors: Kyeongryeol Go
abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.

title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender
authors: Yuzhe Chen and Muxi Diao and Lele Yang and Wenbin Xu and Xuyang Liu and Qile Su and Changyi Liu and Jiankang Chen and Kaiyu Jiang and Haoyu Zhang and Hongyi Fu and Jianxiong Wang and Tianke Zhang and Haonan Fan and Yingxin Li and Bingyi Li and Xu Wang and Xuanyu Zheng and Bin Wen and Tingting Gao and Wentao Zhang and Jiale Cao
abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
authors: Vahid Haratian and Vahid Ansari and Mohammadhossein Malmir and Alois Knoll
abstract: Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present Robo-SWE, a dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28 public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers' fix, and the developers' tests, which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup, resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%. GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.

title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?
authors: Zhiyu Hou and Wen-Jie Shu and Harold Haodong Chen and Weilin Ruan and Chenfei Liao and Liuzhou Zhang and Disen Lan and Xiaogang Xu and Qi Chen and Ser-Nam Lim
abstract: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

title: Agentic Dashboards: A New Design Paradigm for Visual Analytics
authors: Sam Yu-Te Lee and Yun-Hsin Kuo and Kwan-Liu Ma
abstract: Visual analytics systems traditionally combine analytical methods and interactive visualizations into a fixed application specified at the design phase. Coding agents offer a flexible approach: experts could conduct analysis through natural-language instructions. We envision an agentic dashboard as a persistent visual analytics workspace where an agent makes decisions about analytical methods, views, and their coordination within a designer-defined decision space. This approach shifts part of the visualization designer's role from engineering a fixed interface to defining the decisions an agent may make at runtime. We illustrate how such a dashboard could operate with current capabilities and propose criteria for evaluating its behavior and potential failures. As analytical workflows become more fluid and agent-mediated, visualization can help experts maintain awareness, coordinate with agents, and exercise judgment.

title: ControlHarbor: A Benchmark for Control Design by Coding Agents
authors: Jieqiang Wei and Fahad Ali and Jonny Reichwald and Silun Zhang
abstract: LLM agents, i.e., language models run by a harness, can now write, run and debug software autonomously. This raises the question of whether they can also carry out control system design. In this paper, we consider control system design as a task for LLM agents and grade the designed controller as control engineers do: the controller is given in a single Python file mapping measurements to actions, evaluated on held-out seeds against an ordered set of requirements, under specified physical perturbations and structural certificates, without using neural networks. We formulate the task as a chance-constrained feasibility problem and instantiate it in ControlHarbor, a benchmark of 44 tasks over 13 plants, which includes network consensus, vehicle platooning, the MuJoCo hopper, walker and humanoid. The tasks are packaged in the Harbor format, so that any agent harness can be run against them, and the same environments also serve learning algorithms other than LLMs, such as reinforcement learning (RL), under the same evaluation. With ControlHarbor, we observe that the controllers designed by three frontier coding agents, Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5, reach the RL return on every parity task, but only in a minority of sessions. We also observe that the controllers certified for return alone usually fail under perturbations. When robustness is part of the specification, a structured design meets it at the RL return on the humanoid task, where domain-randomised RL does not; under large pushes, domain-randomised RL succeeds and no designed controller does. The benchmark, the controllers, and their grades are released.

title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
authors: NovaSilicon Team
abstract: Coding agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in software development, yet their ability to tackle long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints remains less understood. We study this question through analog circuit layout, which demands domain knowledge, geometric reasoning, and iterative interaction with design and verification tools. We introduce \textbf{AnalogLayoutWorld}, an open-source agent benchmark with 40 expert-reviewed tasks for end-to-end layout generation from fixed transistor-level netlists. It combines an integrated design environment with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification, as well as objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts. Across 13 model--harness configurations, 91.1\% of attempts produce GDS layouts, but only 23.0\% satisfy the benchmark's acceptance criteria. We also evaluate Novara, an internally developed agent system, which achieves the highest reported aggregate score. Our analysis links performance differences to test-time scaling under fixed budgets, suggesting that reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

title: ParseBench-2: Severity-Aware Evaluation of Document Parsing
authors: Pierre-Loïc Doulcet and Boyang Zhang and Sebastián G. Acosta and Sacha Bron and Daniel B. Ospina and Antonio Jimeno Yepes and Nutchapol Dendumrongsup and Simon Suo
abstract: Document-parsing metrics can give high scores to outputs that change important facts and penalize changes that preserve meaning. People can often judge these consequences more easily than they can design a metric to measure them. We introduce a method for developing parsing metrics from severity policies that specify how each error type should affect the score. We express these policies through test scenarios that specify how a metric should behave. We then optimize the metric implementations against these fixed expectations, using coding agents to refine comparison rules, error detectors and weights under human review. This makes stated human priorities an explicit objective of metric design. We apply this method in ParseBench-2, a comprehensive document-parsing benchmark that combines broad capability coverage with metrics calibrated to error severity. It covers 4,317 pages across six dimensions of parsing quality: text, formatting, tables, charts, visual grounding, and forms. We use detailed annotations and targeted difficult cases to check for changed facts, broken structural relationships, and missing content. We take the lower of a parsing score that measures content recovery and a severity cap that penalizes detected errors, so recovering most of a page cannot hide a serious error. Across six severity test suites, our metrics more closely match the expert judgments expressed by the scenario targets than existing metrics and penalize at most 3.4% of the tested benign variations. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation spanning frontier vision-language models, specialized document parsers and open-weight systems, comparing their overall rankings, performance across parsing capabilities and tradeoffs between accuracy and cost.

title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
authors: Haozhe Wang and Lina Chen and Fanqi Wan and Qi Han and Yinmin Zhang and Zheng Ge and Daxin Jiang and Junchi Yan
abstract: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.

title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
authors: Peiwen Li and Harshit Verma and Sophia Zhou and Haiwen Wang and Ngoc Bui and Heng Chang and Fei Fei and David van Dijk and Rex Ying
abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.

title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
authors: Ibragim Badertdinov and Alexander Golubev
abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

title: Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved job-shop benchmark instances
authors: Andre Albrecht and Enzo Morosini Frazzon and Leandro C. Coelho and Bruno Vieira
abstract: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.

title: TelePhysica: Agentic Reconstruction of Physically Interactive Scenes
authors: Ruiqi Shu and Xufeng Zhan and Yuanzhi Liang and Haibin Huang and Chi Zhang and Xuelong Li
abstract: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.

title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams
authors: Issa Sugiura and Taro Makino and Takashi Ishida
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. To construct it, we develop a human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, while a human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. This pipeline adapts to heterogeneous exam formats and reduces the effort of incorporating new exam editions, enabling periodic refreshes that mitigate data contamination. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall, while even the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points. When models can additionally use a terminal and web access, they retrieve the knowledge they lack and every model improves. The gap narrows but about 4 points remain, and the ranking of models stays largely the same, suggesting that knowledge held in the model itself remains valuable even with tools. We release the dataset, the evaluation code, and the construction pipeline.

title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
authors: Hua Yang and Aditya Bhardwaj and Shidong Pan and Bowen Xu
abstract: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.

title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors
authors: Shervin Shahidi and James Poon and Hang Xie and Kenneth O. Xu and Robin Håkanson and Vikram Nair and Jens Pillgram-Larsen and Nachiappan Nagappan
abstract: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus~4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, $p=0.002$) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, $p=0.004$); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.

title: DataTrace: Benchmarking Data Agents for Evidence-Grounded Root-Cause Localization
authors: Tung Sum Thomas Kwok and Xiaotian Lin and Yuyu Luo
abstract: Database agents diagnose pipeline failures, but a correct root cause is trustworthy only when it is supported by evidence the agent inspected. Existing benchmarks usually grade the final query or answer but fail to distinguish an evidence-based diagnosis from an unsupported correct answer. We introduce DataTrace, a benchmark for evidence-grounded root-cause localization over typed graphs of database artifacts. DataTrace uses controlled fault injection to derive root causes and evidence paths within 83 runnable environments without human annotations, and scores root-cause correctness and coverage of the supporting path separately. We also introduce CoSE, a generator-solver protocol in which an external verifier admits reproducible faults and checks both the submitted answer and the inspected evidence. Our evaluation shows that seven proprietary models achieve average root-cause accuracy 48%, with a mean per-model conditional unsupported rate of 18%. Fine-grained analysis shows that this gap varies sharply with fault mechanism, dependency distance, and evidence modality. After in-loop training on a matched held-out batch, the share of grounded correct diagnoses rises from 83.7% to 94.6%, while root-cause accuracy rises from 29.2% to 36.7%. These results show that while final-answer accuracy can hide unsupported diagnoses, evidence coverage provides an actionable signal to improve database agents. Code and data are available at https://hkustdial.github.io/datatrace/.

title: What Moves a LoCoMo Score? Memory Context, Answer Prompts and Judges
authors: Nikhil Kumar Jha and Amitoj Cheema
abstract: LoCoMo is a widely reported benchmark for long-term conversational memory, but published scores mix memory quality with choices of answer prompt, judge and baseline layout that are rarely reported together. We measure how much these choices move a score, and evaluate Becos, a team memory system for coding agents, as a black box under all of them: ten conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts and three LLM judges, against a whole-conversation baseline rerun under identical conditions. Changing only the judge moves a score by up to 7.2 points and changing only the answer prompt by up to 9.3. A blind human check of 150 answers finds the judges reliable when they agree, and the primary judge's errors on disputed answers working against Becos rather than for it. Becos answers from a context with 90% fewer characters than the whole conversation. Its configuration was developed on LoCoMo itself, so there is no held-out set. With gpt-4o-mini answers it scores clearly higher than the whole conversation (79.7 vs 73.0 with the short prompt, paired 95% interval for the difference +3.8 to +9.5; 88.8 vs 77.5 with a step-by-step prompt). With gpt-4.1-mini answers the two score about the same (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1). We release every answer and verdict and the scoring script.

title: Beyond Prompts: Runtime Contracts for Coding Agents
authors: Reda Heddad
abstract: Coding agents act on repositories through shell commands and file edits, and teams steer them with written engineering rules. Industrial settings expect such rules to be enforced and their application to be evidenced, and a rule given as prompt text provides neither. We test whether executable contracts enforced while the agent works reduce rule violations compared with the same rules in the prompt, retrieved as guidance, or checked only after generation. Violations are scored by an oracle whose methods differ from the in-loop checks, and the oracle is validated by two human reviewers and a model reviewer. Across three studies on two model families (240, 112 and 108 runs), enforcement during execution produced no oracle-detected violation in 104 paired runs, against 21 to 55% of runs without rules, and no loss of functional correctness in the two confirmatory studies. In the confirmatory study on tasks aimed at known failure situations (Study 3, protocol hashed before the first run), enforcement lowered the share of violating runs by 31 percentage points relative to no rules (Holm-adjusted p = 0.014); the 17-point difference from prompted rules was not significant (p = 0.12), and neither was any contrast in Study 2, where only 3 of 14 tasks produced a violation. Prompted rules removed some violation types but not recursive deletes of scratch directories, and checks after generation repaired file edits but not commands that had already run. That enforcement satisfies the rules it enforces is expected by construction; what the data add is where prompting falls short, the absence of a functional cost, and the limits of the rules and of the oracle themselves. The studies use low-cost models and one small fixture.

title: Compositional Exploits in Autonomous Coding Agents: Attack Mechanics and Ephemeral Defense
authors: Deep Shah and Nehal Kathrotia
abstract: Autonomous coding agents (such as Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenHands) rely on third-party tools to inspect files, run commands, and call external APIs. Today's security auditors evaluate these tools almost entirely in isolation: static linters and AST checkers verify that each individual tool contains no malicious code at installation time. In this paper, we show that isolated tool auditing is fundamentally flawed. We expose compositional exploits in autonomous coding agents, an emergent vulnerability class where an agent chains individually harmless tools to execute an unauthorized attack. Much like code-reuse attacks in binary exploitation, this threat requires no malware; instead, the agent stitches together legitimate tool operations across turns over shared workspace files, environment variables, and chat memory. Across a 560-task benchmark suite (360 exploit tasks across 8 hazard classes and 200 benign developer and cloud workflows), unprotected frontier models (Gemini 3.5, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash) execute compositional exploit chains with a 72.9% to 84.5% success rate, while five leading single-tool pre-distribution scanners exhibit a 0% detection rate across all constituent tools. To eliminate compositional exploits, we present CompGuard, an OS-grounded defense uniting two planes: (1) a Cognitive Control Plane that issues single-skill capability leases and tracks dataflow provenance, and (2) an OS Kernel Enforcement Layer using Linux Landlock LSM v4, seccomp-BPF socket filters, and an ephemeral loopback proxy to close the invocation gap. CompGuard achieves a 100% Defense Block Rate (0.0% to 0.8% pre-teardown Net ASR) at 61.4 microseconds interposition overhead, preserves a 98.0% solve rate on benign developer workflows, and triggers zero false alarms across 615 real cloud diagnostic calls.

title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations
authors: Xinping Lei and Minghao Liu and Ruijie Zhu and Xiaohui Hu and Xingqiao Li and Ao Zhang and Wenhao Chai and Han Li and Tao Wang and Jingyuan Zhang and Enduo Zhao and Yunfeng Shi and Yiming Liang and Zetao Yang and Xingjian Wang and Yifan Yao and Xinkai Ma and Yingru Li and Tianhan Yang and Huan Zhou and Weiran Shi and Shen Yan and Jiaheng Liu and Stephen Huang and Eli Cheung and Weihao Xuan
abstract: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
authors: Siqiao Xue and Ziyin Zhang and Zihan Liao and Jin Qin and Yixiang Mu and Hang Yu
abstract: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with \texttt{grep}. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over $91$ repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
authors: Bowen Liu and Yuhan Li and Nuo Chen and Weile Luo and Miao Peng and Qintong Zhang and Qifan Zhang and Jia Li and Ziqi Gao and Lydell Huang
abstract: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
authors: Yuhang He and Yanyu Chen and Chuanzhe Guo and Jie Zhu and Zichen Tian and Hongyu Ge and Zixuan Ren and Huang He and Bingjin Chen and Junyuan Shang and Shuohuan Wang and Yongqi Zhang and Irwin King and Jing Liu
abstract: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

title: Evaluation-Free Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents
authors: Zhe Ren and Guowei Rong and Yimeng Chen and Nanbo Li and Piotr Piękos and Mateusz Ostaszewski and Dandan Guo and Jürgen Schmidhuber
abstract: Recent self-improving coding agents have achieved strong benchmark performance by iteratively modifying their own executable implementations. A common pattern uses downstream task-derived evidence to decide which candidates or lineages continue evolving, which we term evaluate-and-select. Obtaining this signal requires repeatedly executing evolved agents on downstream tasks, so broader exploration incurs increasing evaluation cost, while repeated optimization against a fixed evaluation distribution may encourage benchmark-specific adaptation. We ask: can coding agents self-improve without downstream task evaluation inside the evolution loop? We introduce Explore-then-Integrate (ELITE), which integrates implementation mechanisms rather than selecting a single exploratory child to continue the lineage. At each generation, ELITE proposes diverse focused improvements, implements them independently from the same parent, and inspects the resulting programs to identify complementary, redundant, and conflicting mechanisms before reimplementing a compatible subset as one coherent descendant. No downstream task outcomes or task-solving trajectories of evolved candidates are used to guide evolution; only deterministic checks of structural and operational validity are used inside the loop. On SWE-bench Pro, ELITE improves the initial agent from 60.0% to 85.6%, compared with 86.7% for the Darwin Godel Machine (DGM) and 88.3% for the Huxley-Godel Machine (HGM), while using zero candidate task evaluations and reducing observed wall-clock evolution time by 8.8x and 3.2x, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. In cross-benchmark transfer without further adaptation, ELITE averages 73.3% on SWE-bench Verified and 69.3% on Polyglot. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of coding-agent self-improvement without downstream candidate task evaluation in our setting.

title: From Repositories to Training Environments: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding Agents with Environment Evolution Loop
authors: Yang Tian and Tianyu Zheng and Xiyuan Yang and Yaxin Du and Chengran Yang and Bo Zhao and Jian Yang and Bryan Dai
abstract: Training coding agents for long-horizon tasks requires environments with verifiable feedback. Existing pipelines often follow a linear process that ends with validation, establishing usability but providing little guidance on improving training value. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) often requires model rollouts or model training followed by downstream evaluation, with costs and feedback delays amplified on long-horizon tasks. How can we use timely, reliable proxy signals to improve training value and synthesize environments at scale? We present RepoFactory, an automated pipeline that converts real repositories into verifiable environments where agents build complete projects from scratch given a language specification. Its Environment Evolution Loop optimizes a multiplicative objective combining validity, structural coupling, and implementation scope through proxy feedback. RepoFactory produces 10,159 environments across 17 software domains. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on these environments yields RepoHorizen-35B-A3B, which achieves gains of 22.6 percentage points on NL2Repo-Bench and 8.5 points on average across five benchmarks covering long-horizon coding and agentic tasks in real-world production settings, compared with 17.5 and 6.4 points without environment evolution. These results highlight the training value of RepoFactory environments and the additional gains from the Environment Evolution Loop.

title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
authors: Jayanaka Dantanarayana and Savini Kashmira and Xiaoyu Ma and Malitha and Malitha Prabhashana and Lingjia Tang and Jason Mars
abstract: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

title: ExRel: Learning Directed Reuse Relevance between Rich-Text K-12 Question Images with Executable Relation Contracts
authors: Xuexin Liu and Zengyi Wo and Shiyu Zhang and Suqi Cheng and Daiting Shi and Xiuyi Chen
abstract: In K-12 education, question images combine text, mathematical expressions, diagrams, and diverse layouts. Variations in wording, conditions, answer options, or task scope can substantially alter their reuse utility despite visual similarity. We formulate this problem as directed reuse relevance, grading candidate utility as Strong, Medium, or Weak. However, generic similarity scores overlook task-specific reuse requirements, while natural supervision is dominated by Strong relations and lacks fine-grained coverage. We propose ExRel, an agentic, code-grounded framework for controllable and verifiable visual data synthesis. It reconstructs real questions into editable HTML/CSS seeds and compiles 15 relation subtypes into executable contracts specifying permitted edits, protected invariants, and query-candidate direction. Synthesized pairs undergo deterministic DOM/render validation and target-hidden, evidence-assisted review, with bounded repair before mild photographic degradation. Only rendered images are used for downstream training. Experiments show that ExRel supervision outperforms size-matched natural data and count- and class-matched replay, particularly on Medium relations, while maintaining comparable query-level ranking performance and improving robustness to visual degradation. Construction ablations demonstrate higher valid yield and fewer false admissions than less structured baselines. Human audits confirm 98.0% post-admission validity, while ExRel achieves a lower per-accepted-pair cost than outsourced annotation (0.70 vs. 1.10 RMB). Downstream answer routing further demonstrates the practical utility of the synthesized supervision.

title: Beyond Leaderboard Ranks: Selecting Software Engineering Agents Under Budget Constraints
authors: Srinath Srinivasan and Tim Menzies
abstract: Teams that adopt LLM agents for issue resolution must decide which agent to pay for, and how much to spend finding out. Leaderboard ranks give weak evidence for this decision. Accuracy differences may be statistically unresolved, reported costs may be inconsistent, and evaluating candidate agents can itself be expensive. We investigate budget-constrained agent selection using 58,197 run--task records extracted from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL), focusing on SWE-bench and six additional benchmarks. Across seven benchmarks, 27 of 35 steps along the accuracy--cost Pareto frontiers are statistically unresolved. On SWE-bench, a run costing $34.16 trails the $170.78 leader by 14.6 percentage points, but the available tasks cannot statistically distinguish their accuracy. Reported costs also differ from standardized token-based estimates by up to 11.7x, while selective task evaluation can bias estimates of full-benchmark execution cost. We therefore compare evaluation strategies under explicit evaluation budgets and deployment-cost caps. Under advance knowledge of task costs, successive halving reaches our uncertainty-aware selection target on SWE-bench using 6.6% of exhaustive evaluation spend, achieving the lowest cost on six of seven benchmarks and tying on the seventh. Its advantage narrows when task costs are unknown before execution or exact-best selection is required.
