Our findings motivate decision-oriented agent evaluation that accounts for accuracy uncertainty, validates execution costs, and compares complex selection methods against simple adaptive allocation.

title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
authors: Gil Pasternak and AJ Langley and Tom Yotam and Ellie Kitanidis
abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
authors: Minghui Zhao and Yiming Li and Sophie Zhu and Maxwell Khor and Lauren Ouyang and Hai "Helen" Li and Yiran Chen and Tingjun Chen
abstract: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
authors: Alan Subedi and Avhishek Biswas and Apala Pramanik and Amlan Balabantaray and Mikhail Titov and Santosh Pitla and Ozgur Kilic and Mehmet C. Vuran
abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
authors: Gengyue Dong and Ye Wei and Zheng Zhu and Yidong Han and Jiale Miao and Xiaojun Jia and Guanghui Li
abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
authors: Allen G. Roush and Minh Nhat Nguyen and Ravid Shwartz-Ziv and Judah Goldfeder and Sanjay Basu
abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

title: HandRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Hand Pose Estimation
authors: Zhekai Wang and Luqing Luo and Wenhao Yao and Junjie Lu and Huanan Zhu and Feifei Gao and Yuhua Jiang
abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.

title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
authors: Kaixin Li and Meng Luo and Yanlin Li and Yuchen Tian and Xiang Liu and Xiangru Jian and Yan Yang and Zhiheng Xi and Yang Zhang and Ziyang Luo and Mingfei Cheng and Hongzhan Lin
abstract: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
authors: Junyi Shen and Yao Lu
abstract: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.

title: MCP-based AI coding agent Integrating Static Analysis for Web Accessibility Error Correction
journal: 2025 TRON Symposium (TRONSHOW)
authors: Y. Higuchi and J. -E. Kim and M. Bessho
abstract: While ensuring web accessibility is becoming a legal obligation, 94.8% of the top one million websites violate WCAG standards, highlighting the need for more efficient implementation support in development environments. This paper proposes a novel approach to ensuring web accessibility using general-purpose AI coding agents by providing them with appropriate contextual information for accessibility error correction through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. This approach enables integration of Biome’s static analysis with the flexible code-base understanding capabilities of AI coding agents to efficiently produce WCAG-compliant fixes. Adopting the MCP architecture enables uniform use across various AI coding agent environments, such as Claude Code and Roo Code. We conducted experiments using an AI coding agent with four different LLM backends on a common test case and demonstrated the feasibility of our approach.
keywords: Protocols;Law;Biological system modeling;Static analysis;Encoding;Error correction codes;Servers;Artificial intelligence;Standards;Context modeling;Web accessibility;LLM;WCAG;Model Context Protocol;AI coding agents;Static Analysis

title: GHAgentFiles: A dataset of coding agent file histories in GitHub repositories
journal: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
authors: G. Cardoen and T. Mens and A. Decan
abstract: Since the introduction of coding-specific LLMs in the early 2020s, coding agents have become increasingly popular in collaborative software development projects. Since 2025, it is common practice to specify context files that provide additional context to coding agents about the project structure, development commands, coding conventions, and so on. To enable large-scale empirical studies of collaborative GitHub repositories involving coding agents, we provide a dataset of context, skill and subagent files and an open-source tool to identify and extract such files automatically. Out of an initial list of 165K+ repositories, we identify 27K+ repositories with coding agent files for six major agents (Claude, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Windsurf and Cursor), resulting in 142K+ distinct file histories and 401K+ revisions covering their evolution. We conduct a preliminary observational analysis on this large dataset and present some perspectives to the research community on how to use this dataset for future empirical studies.
keywords: Context;Codes;Encoding;Software development management;History;Printing;Electronic mail;Tools;Evolution (biology);Software;dataset;coding agent;context file;collaborative software development;empirical software engineering

title: Evolution Context Gap: An Empirical Study of Agent Manifests
journal: 2026 23rd International Joint Conference on Computer Science and Software Engineering (JCSSE)
authors: N. Chondamrongkul and W. Rueangsirarak and P. Jakkaew
abstract: AI coding agents—Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor—increasingly rely on developer-authored instruction les (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md, etc.) to understand project context. These agent manifests have not been systematically studied. We present the first large-scale content analysis of 80 real-world manifests drawn from five agent types using a six-category taxonomy and a three-model LLM classifier with majority-vote consensus. Workflow & Process dominates (present in 96.2% of manifests, 43.5% mean character fraction), while evolution context—information about how the software changes over time—is largely absent: 73.8% of manifests contain no evolution content, and none references Lehman’s laws of software evolution. A single significant project-level correlation emerges: manifests in more law-conformant projects contain more coding-style guidance (ρ = 0.431, p = 0.040, n=23). These findings characterise a systematic evolution context gap that leaves agents architecture-blind and motivate automated manifest enrichment tooling.
keywords: Evolution (biology);Context;Law;Codes;Encoding;Modeling;Labeling;Printing;Complexity theory;Artificial intelligence;agent manifests;AI coding agents;software evolution;content analysis;CLAUDE.md;empirical study

title: Agentic AI for Platform Engineering: Rethinking developer platforms with agentic AI, RAG, MCP, and governed autonomous operations
authors: Tiago Miguel Reichert and Lucas Soriano Alves Duarte and Jaime Nagase and Chris Aniszczyk
abstract: Build AI-driven platforms with RAG, MCP, governed agents, and observability, while seeing how Claude Code, Kiro, and Codex CLI fit into the shift from personal coding agents to governed platform agentsKey FeaturesEnd-to-end coverage from AI-enhanced developer portals to governed agentic operationsApply agentic AI patterns for governed remediation, observability, and human-in-the-loop controlGenerate infrastructure-as-code and CI/CD artifacts through conversational AI interfacesBook DescriptionPlatform engineers today face a growing challenge: developer platforms must scale faster than teams can maintain them. This book shows how to embed GenAI, RAG, MCP, and governed agents into developer platforms while preserving delivery and governance practices. The book moves from platform engineering and AIOps foundations to organizational knowledge, conversational interfaces, and agentic operations. Along the way, it places Claude Code, Kiro, and Codex CLI within this evolution, showing how these tools connect to the shift toward governed agents across platforms and organizations. You will build RAG pipelines, connect platform capabilities through MCP, and explore natural-language generation of Terraform and Kubernetes artifacts alongside CI/CD use cases. Hands-on chapters use Backstage, GitOps, Argo CD, Strands, and Langfuse to demonstrate assistants, governed pull-request changes, observability, audit trails, and operational agents. You will also learn when single- or multi-agent designs are appropriate, evaluate build-versus-buy choices, and address prompt injection, memory poisoning, identity abuse, and compliance. By the end, you will be able to design AI-enhanced developer platforms that improve self-service while keeping high-impact actions observable, auditable, and subject to human approval where risk demands it.What you will learnBuild RAG systems grounded in organizational knowledgeBuild governed agents that propose changes through pull requestsConnect conversational workflows to platform tools with MCPExplore where Claude Code and Kiro fit in agentic platform workflowsTrace agent activity and maintain auditable operational recordsSecure agent workflows with guardrails, identity, and compliance controlsCompare personal and production agents with governed tool accessEvaluate build-versus-buy choices for AI platform capabilitiesWho this book is forThis book is for platform engineers, SREs, DevOps professionals, and cloud architects who want to integrate GenAI and agentic AI into internal developer platforms. If you are responsible for building or maintaining internal platforms and want to improve developer self-service, operational intelligence, and governed automation, this book is for you. Technical leaders driving AI adoption within engineering teams will also find valuable strategic guidance. Basic familiarity with cloud computing, infrastructure as code, Kubernetes, CI/CD, and DevOps practices is assumed.

title: Uncovering AGENTS.md: What Testing Guidance Open Source Projects Provide to Coding Agents
journal: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Source Code Analysis & Manipulation (SCAM)
authors: B. Ardic and M. Olsthoorn and A. Zaidman
abstract: Agentic coding tools increasingly operate inside software repositories, where their behavior is shaped not only by model capabilities but also by repository context. An emerging form to provide such context is agent context files, also known as AI guidance files (e.g., AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md), which can encode project commands, conventions, and development expectations. In this paper, we study how open-source projects organize these guidance files and how they communicate testing expectations to coding agents. We analyze repositories from AIDev-pop, a collection of popular GitHub repositories with observed agent-authored pull requests. We first mine root-level AI guidance files and any Markdown files they explicitly reference to characterize repository-level organization and delegation. We find that root-level guidance is concentrated in generic AGENTS.md files and Claude-specific files, and that root guidance is not always self-contained: many repositories refer to additional resources. We then manually analyze testing guidance in a stratified sample of 300 repositories, covering 626 Markdown files and more than 3,300 coded quotations. In our sample, testing guidance is common: 249 of the 300 repositories include test commands, helping agents execute repository-specific tests. Less frequent themes on testing guidance are related to strategy, mentality, mocking, coverage, avoidance, and naming convention expectations. Overall, our results show that AI guidance files are currently mostly used to expose testing infrastructure to coding agents, but are less consistently used to make maintainer expectations about good tests explicit.
keywords: Artificial intelligence;Codes;Poles and zeros;Testing;Encoding;Printing;Tools;Documentation;Software development management;Conferences;Software engineering;agentic coding;AI agents;AI guidance;software testing;open-source software

title: Execution Control Harness for Governed LLM-Based Code Generation
journal: 2026 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
authors: M. Takeda and Y. Funaya and O. Harriet and R. Mibe and H. Kanuka
abstract: LLM-based coding agents have strong potential for automating software development, but their direct application remains fragile under long and complex requirements. Specification omissions are common, and autonomous local fixes can trigger cascading regressions. In a preliminary experiment, implementing a single business function using a standard specification-driven approach required 65 interaction rounds and approximately 9 hours of manual correction.In this paper, we propose an execution control harness that tightly couples LLM-based code generation with governed execution. Implemented as a YAML-based workflow DSL, the harness integrates mechanically scoped reasoning, deterministic validation gates, automated Git-based rollback, and hybrid human-agent control.A case study on a real-world insurance application of approximately 30 KLOC suggests that the proposed approach helps suppress specification omissions and regression chains. Under comparable conditions, the number of correction iterations was reduced from 65 to 3, and total development time decreased from 9.0 to 0.5 hours. These results indicate that reliable AI-driven software development requires not only capable agents but also execution control architectures that govern the generation process.
keywords: Modeling;Large language models;Cognition;Cognitive systems;Codes;DSL;Design methodology;Manuals;Software;Printing;LLM-based code generation;software engineering;AI-assisted development;workflow systems;domain-specific languages;software quality

title: Spec-Driven AI: A Multiagent Framework for Specification-Centric SDLC Automation
journal: 2026 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
authors: J. C. Bello and D. Fazzioni and V. M. A. De Lima and T. N. Kudo and A. Da Silva Soares
abstract: AI coding assistants are transforming software development, but most approaches remain code-centric and weakly connected to requirements, specifications, architectural decisions, organizational standards, and quality gates. This paper presents Spec-Driven AI, a multiagent framework for specification-centric Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) automation. The framework combines an SDLC orchestrator, specialized lifecycle agents, human-in-the-loop gates, auditable artifact generation, and a Pattern Manager / Context Platform that provides governed context through repository indexing, document retrieval, knowledge graph extraction, adherence validation, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. Spec-Driven AI treats specifications as verifiable contracts and uses agents to coordinate discovery, specification, design, planning, implementation support, testing, review, and traceability. We describe the architecture, implementation, and demonstration scenario showing how a project is registered, indexed, governed, and used to prepare structured context for SDLC agents. Screencast: https://youtu.be/w4QT-nrRgNo.
keywords: Context;Codes;Indexes;Indexing;Artificial intelligence;Modeling;Tools;Printing;Large language models;Evolution (biology);Spec-Driven Development;Multiagent Systems;AI-Assisted Software Engineering;Software Maintenance and Evolution;SDLC Automation

title: A Knowledge Engineering Framework for AI-Driven Software Development: Harness, Guardrail, and AI-Native Knowledge DevOps
journal: 2026 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA)
authors: K. Watanabe and H. Ogawa and S. Ito and T. Nakazawa and K. Tsuru
abstract: Development-time knowledge—design rationale, architectural decisions, domain constraints, hard-won lessons—generated during AI-driven software development is largely ephemeral, lost between agent sessions. We propose a knowledge engineering framework whose guiding principle is pervasive AI participation—an aspirational design stance in which the agent accompanies the development workflow as broadly as practical and externalizes what it observes into machine-readable artifacts. The framework casts an Effective Agent as Foundation Model + (Harness ∥ Guardrail): two parallel operational concerns—Harness (course-setting; Knowledge, Skills, Stakeholder personas, Runtime/loader) and Guardrail (deviation detection; static analysis, automated tests, an adversarial review-gate drawing on a heterogeneous foundation-model family (untested), post-push review). A separate, external meta-process, AI-Native Knowledge DevOps (Capture/Refine/Create/Apply, GitOps-versioned, agent-loop driven), refines them across sessions: capture Guardrail findings and re-inject refined artifacts into both Harness and Guardrail. Adopting ADRs, GitOps, and concurrent harness-engineering corpora (AGENTS.md, plans, post-integration sensors, AI-rule promotion [1]–[3]) as foundations rather than novelty, our narrower contribution is a four-cell Harness, a Guardrail panel at parity, and a dual-target refinement loop (a design hypothesis we present, not an evaluated effect). A 142-day, 297-commit longitudinal experience report (a marketsizing tool for business planning under the TAM/SAM/SOM framework, built with Claude Code plus an OpenAI Codex CLI review-gate) illustrates the framework: 9,441 LOC, 441 tests, 14 knowledge documents (7,349 lines), and 92 issues (78 filed via the agent’s issue-lifecycle Skill). Commit-history analysis shows 63% of commits on the agent-loaded artifacts are maintenance-class rather than purely additive—we report this as a descriptive number, not as evidence the cycle caused the share, since the case is N=1 with the developer overlapping the framework authors.

title: Specifications as Governance Artifacts: Human–AI Collaboration and Oversight for AI-Generated Code
journal: 2026 IEEE Conference on Generative AI for Secure Systems (GAISS)
authors: N. Garg and R. Mohindra and S. Maru
abstract: AI coding assistants now write a large share of production software, and they write it fast. This shifts software engineering from writing code to governing it: deciding who is accountable for AI-generated behavior, how divergence from intent is detected, and how humans and models divide the labor of oversight. Most teams lack a structured answer, and AI-generated code reaches production carrying security defects, functional bugs, and behavioral drift. We present a specification-driven governance framework that treats the specification as the primary governance artifact and the shared contract for human–AI collaboration. The framework adds a specification review gate modeled on the high-level and low-level design (HLD/LLD) reviews teams already trust; it then treats the approved specification, HLD, and LLD as an explicit, auditable baseline against which generated code is checked for drift, routing every flagged drift to a human for reconciliation. We make the collaboration concrete—defining author, reviewer, model, and reconciler roles as a responsibility assignment (RACI) and specifying the audit trail the baseline produces—and align the control points to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act. We evaluate with a controlled within-subject human study of five reviewers performing baseline-anchored versus code-only drift review on real AI-generated services, and—to check robustness in a separate population—a large automated-reviewer replication (three models, 90 machine reviews) of the same design. The human study reports an honest, sharp result: an approved specification did not increase the number of drifts reviewers caught (recall 0.53 vs $0.52, \mathrm{p}=0.69$), but it made findings attributable—reviewers tied 81% of findings to a named requirement versus 0% without a baseline $(\mathrm{p}=0.043)$—and raised confidence, at a significant effort cost $(\approx 48 vs 27 min, p = 0.043)$. The automated replication produced a similar pattern. Recall remained essentially unchanged $(\mathrm{p}=0.95)$, whereas attribution increased from 0.00 to 0.67 (p < 10-4) for all models. We observed this result across reviewers rather than for only one reviewer, suggesting that the effect is associated with the review setup rather than an individual reviewer's behavior. The anonymized artifact released with the study includes the complete set of materials.

title: Methods and Techniques of Agentic Software Engineering: A Systematic Literature Review
journal: IEEE Access
authors: N. Otoum and N. Elkhalili
abstract: The development of agentic software engineering (ASE) is shifting the software development process, specifically by adopting autonomous agents into the fundamental software development process, where autonomous agents using large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) make decisions, write code, and collaborate across the entire software development lifecycle. The systematic review is a summary of literature on the agentic software engineering methodologies, frameworks, and techniques published in 2022-2025. We identify and compare methods based on autonomous coding, multi-agent systems, iterative refinement, and human-agent collaboration, drawing on 61 high-quality studies. We find that LLM-based agents show substantial potential in automated software engineering and that recent work is exploring new trends in agent cooperation, reasoning systems, and tool integration. We recognize such key challenges as the coordination procedures, reliability, explainability, and the ethical issues. This review characterizes the emerging role of agentic software engineering in improving the productivity of developers, the quality of their code, and the automation of their processes, and it offers a structured roadmap for future research. With the rapid evolution of the field, agentic approaches will tend to transform the conception, creation, and maintenance of software and provide more autonomous, adaptive, and intelligent systems.

title: Exploring Autonomous Agents: A Closer Look at Why They Fail When Completing Tasks

abstract: Autonomous agent systems powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in automating complex tasks. However, current evaluations largely rely on success rates without systematically analyzing the interactions, communication mechanisms, and failure causes within these systems. To bridge this gap, we present a benchmark of 34 representative programmable tasks designed to rigorously assess autonomous agents. Using this benchmark, we evaluate three popular open-source agent frameworks combined with two LLM backbones, observing a task completion rate of approximately 50%. Through in-depth failure analysis, we develop a three-tier taxonomy of failure causes aligned with task phases, highlighting planning errors, task execution issues, and incorrect response generation. Based on these insights, we propose actionable improvements to enhance agent planning and self-diagnosis capabilities. Our failure taxonomy, together with mitigation advice, provides an empirical foundation for developing more robust and effective autonomous agent systems in the future.

title: Designing Autonomous AI Agents for Code Generation, Refactoring, and Maintenance in Agile Software Engineering
journal: 2026 3rd International Conference on Emerging Trends in Engineering and Medical Sciences (ICETEMS)

abstract: This paper suggests a self-organizing multi-agent AI system, which would be used to automate a code generation process, refactor and software maintenance in agile development environments. The first one is the increased productivity of developers, the minimization of technical debt, and high-quality software through facilitating AI-driven, sprint-paced development processes. To do this, the study uses the Code Search Net data set as the sole data set, which implies the high-quality large consistent and high-volume training corpus of more than six million code-documentation pairs of a variety of programming languages. This is achieved by preparing the dataset to be advanced learned by preprocessing and annotating it in a strict pipeline of preprocessing and annotation that includes AST parsing, tokenizer standardization, semantic alignment and automated metadata annotation of the dataset. Methodology This paper presents a new three-agent architecture, Planner, Coder and Reviewer Agents, coupled by a common memory state and reinforced by supervised learning, reinforcement learning and behavior cloning. The system is also tested with multi-layered metrics, e.g. code quality, refactoring effectiveness, maintenance accuracy, workflow-level Agile performance indicators. It is shown that the system shows significant performance improvements compared to the leading baseline models, e.g. Codex, CodeT5, and Code BERT. The suggested framework has a BLEU score of 93.4, Refactoring Quality Score of 95.1 and a Bug-Fix Accuracy of 91.7. It also has a very low technical debt, with a Technical Debt Reduction Index of 89.6, and can execute programs more efficiently with an Execution Efficiency Gain of 41.8. These results prove the fact that the multi-agent design gives meaningful contributions to the contextual reasoning, structural code optimization, and long-term maintainability. This novelty is made through sprint conscious, autonomously communicating AI agents that recreate workflows of real developers, allowing self-enhancing, scaling, and productioncapable automation over contemporary Agile software engineering practices.

abstract: AMASES are a revolutionary approach to automating the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) in a system of intelligent agents working collaboratively. The AMASES framework proposed obtained better accuracy of task completion (97.4%), accuracy of code generation (96.8%), defect detection rate (95.9%), software quality (97.2%), and deployment success rate (98.1%), than existing frameworks such as ChatDev, AgentVerse, MetaGPT, and MARE. title: Graph-Driven Meta-Agents: Integrating Model Context Protocol and LangGraph for Autonomous Software Engineering Agent Generation
journal: IEEE Access
authors: R. Gamidi and A. Vinitha Chowdary and T. Muppala and V. S. S. A. Babu and S. Santhanalakshmi
abstract: Developing autonomous artificial intelligence agents that can reason, use tools, and coordinate multi-step workflows remains a software engineering challenge. Many existing systems use reactive loops or manually specified workflows, which can make state management, termination, and refinement difficult to inspect. This research proposes a graph-driven Meta-Agent architecture that treats agent generation as a compilation process and transforms high-level intent into structured executable graphs. The evaluated implementation combines LangGraph orchestration, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and confidence-guided Critic–Refiner routing. Under a fixed language-model configuration, we evaluated the Full System and five matched controls on 240 paired software-engineering tasks. The Full System completed 220 tasks (91.7%), compared with 156 (65.0%) for a ReAct baseline, 168 (70.0%) without RAG, 188 (78.3%) without refinement, 193 (80.4%) with static rather than MCP-based tool discovery, and 200 (83.3%) without DSPy prompt optimization. Continuity-corrected McNemar tests with Holm adjustment found each paired difference significant ( $p \leq 0.0051$ ). The task-level outcomes are supplied as supplementary material. These results are limited to the evaluated task suite and fixed configuration, but provide controlled evidence for the contributions of graph orchestration, retrieval, refinement, tool discovery, and prompt optimization.

abstract: Autonomous agents are becoming common in software development, but they often struggle to maintain context in large, changing codebases. To solve this, we propose CA-SAF (Codebase-Aware Self-Adapting Framework), a multi-agent system designed to fix this architectural "blindness" by actively retrieving precise code details. Our core innovation is ZSDM (Zero-Shot Dependency Mapping). This hybrid method combines AST parsing with strict LLM extraction to map every entity and relationship into a queryable Knowledge Graph. By using structured code summaries, we achieved roughly 80% data compression, ensuring the context remains efficient. We benchmarked the system against GPT-4o, LLaMA 3.1, and Claude 3 Opus. We found that Claude 3 Opus, with its 200,000 - token window, slightly outperformed the others (capped at 128,000) on complex, non-local mapping tasks. Over a six-month operational study, using CA-SAF led to a measurable drop in both Cycle Time and Lead Time for maintenance work. Crucially, the framework used this codebase awareness to balance speed with quality, actively reducing the number of critical bugs that high-speed LLM generation often introduces.

abstract: As software development becomes intelligent and more autonomous, Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Agentic AI are gaining interest as a means to automate complex software development tasks. The existing studies are scattered over RL-based code generation, program repair, testing, debugging, task planning, software maintenance, and autonomous AI agents, and it is hard to have a systematic understanding of their models, applications, capabilities, and research trends. This study conducts a systematic analysis of the current and available studies on RL models and Agentic AI applications in SD, based on the RL algorithms, agent architectures, software engineering tasks, datasets, evaluation metrics, and outcomes reported. It classifies conventional RL, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and advanced policy- and value-based approaches and investigates the planning and reasoning capabilities, as well as the use of tools, memory, feedback and multi-agent collaboration by Agentic AI in software development tasks. The results have shown that the use of RL and Agentic AI can enhance the quality of code generation, automated testing, defect detection, program repair, task planning, and increase efficiency in the development process, and that agentic architectures offer more autonomy and adaptability than traditional approaches to code generation and automation. However, issues of design of rewards, computational costs, reliability, control of hallucinations, standardized benchmarks, security and reproducibility are yet to be addressed. title: A Decision Framework for Paradigm-Aware Quantum Code Generation in Autonomous Agent Systems
journal: IEEE Access
authors: T. Cervinski and C. Toma and M. Zurini and C. Brandas and L. Morogan
abstract: Cloud platforms have made quantum hardware accessible for research, while autonomous agents powered by large language models are increasingly used to generate code. When such an agent receives a computational problem, however, it often cannot determine whether quantum computing offers a real benefit or whether the problem is better suited to classical hardware. To address this gap, this article proposes a three-stage decision framework. The first stage extracts structural features from the problem description: problem type, search space size, and the presence of a verification oracle. The second stage assigns a quantum advantage classification from established properties of algorithms suited to noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The third stage verifies whether the resulting circuit can be executed on real hardware. Circuit generation is implemented for Grover’s search, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm, and the variational quantum eigensolver, and evaluated on a simulator under six noise channels. An ablation study compares three classifiers on a benchmark of 15 standard and 12 adversarial descriptions: the deterministic framework, a feedforward network trained by back-propagation, and a standalone language model. Their aggregate accuracy is within sampling variation, yet they fail on categorically different problems, and the learned classifier never succeeds where reasoning about problem scale is required. The feasibility gate is further validated against circuits compiled for the coupling map and native gates of a 127-qubit device, showing the accuracy of analytic resource estimates to be strongly algorithm dependent. The implementation is validated with 119 automated tests at 96% code coverage and demonstrated through integration with an autonomous agent platform.

abstract: AI coding agents can solve a large fraction of real-world software engineering tasks, yet the complexity and maintainability of their patches remain poorly understood and largely uncontrolled. We evaluated three frontier models under control and Wily-feedback conditions. A single round of Wily feedback significantly reduces cyclomatic complexity by 20–31% and cognitive complexity by 39–54% across all three models.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now assist with coding, testing, documentation, debugging, and operations, yet enterprise teams often deploy these tools as isolated assistants. title: A 3-Layer Agentic Model for Nonfunctional Requirements in Software Engineering
journal: 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering Workshops (ASEW)
authors: E. Zabardast and T. Vieira and T. Gorschek
abstract: Modern software-intensive systems must address a wide range of nonfunctional requirements (NFRs)—such as security, compliance, and maintainability—that are critical for the long-term success of the system. With the rise of large-language-model-based agents, software engineering is entering an “agentic” era where AI components are not only tools but collaborators in development processes. However, leveraging these agents introduces dual challenges: ensuring that AI components themselves meet quality standards (e.g., compliance, security, maintainability), and harnessing AI effectively to support systemlevel NFR assurance. Our perspective explicitly spans both SE4AI, where AI components such as agents are engineered and subjected to quality assurance and AI4SE, where AI agents support the engineering of software-intensive systems. While these are conceptually distinct, our model addresses both in a unified way. This position paper introduces a conceptual, domain-agnostic three-layer model—comprising Data, Agent, and Perspective layers—for systematically embedding AI agents into NFR assurance across the software lifecycle. The model explicitly captures two complementary viewpoints: Quality for AI (ensuring AI agents are trustworthy and maintainable) and AI for Quality (using agents to support system NFRs). Through illustrative examples in compliance, security, and maintainability, the paper demonstrates how this model can guide researchers and practitioners in designing agent-based approaches to software quality. We argue that this model not only clarifies the dual roles of AI in software engineering but also provides a foundation for responsible, scalable, and effective integration of AI into NFR assurance.

title: From LLM Reasoning to Autonomous AI Agents: A Comprehensive Review
journal: IEEE Access
authors: M. A. Ferrag and N. Tihanyi and M. Debbah
abstract: Large language models and autonomous AI agents have evolved rapidly, resulting in a diverse array of evaluation benchmarks, frameworks, and collaboration protocols. Driven by the growing need for standardized evaluation and integration, we systematically consolidate these fragmented efforts into a unified framework. However, the landscape remains fragmented and lacks a unified taxonomy or comprehensive survey. Therefore, we present a side-by-side comparison of benchmarks developed between 2019 and 2025 that evaluate these models and agents across multiple domains. In addition, we propose a taxonomy of approximately 60 benchmarks that cover general and academic knowledge reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, code generation and software engineering, factual grounding and retrieval, domain-specific evaluations, multimodal and embodied tasks, task orchestration, and interactive assessments. Furthermore, we review AI-agent frameworks introduced between 2023 and 2025 that integrate large language models with modular toolkits to enable autonomous decision-making and multi-step reasoning. Moreover, we present real-world applications of autonomous AI agents in materials science, biomedical research, academic ideation, software engineering, synthetic data generation, chemical reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, geographic information systems, multimedia, healthcare, and finance. We then survey key agent-to-agent collaboration protocols, namely the Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and the Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A). Finally, we discuss recommendations for future research, focusing on advanced reasoning strategies, failure modes in multi-agent LLM systems, automated scientific discovery, dynamic tool integration via reinforcement learning, integrated search capabilities, and security vulnerabilities in agent protocols.

abstract: Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) perform well in simulated environments but struggle under real-world uncertainties. This paper introduces a noise-aware, closed-loop domain randomization framework to evaluate and improve the robustness of cloud-based embodied agents. Our method injects controlled noise-such as sensor errors, command distortions, and object displacements-into the VirtualHome simulator, forcing agents to recover using real-time feedback and replanning. We test five LLM-based agents on 88 tasks under clean and noisy settings. Results show a consistent drop in executability ($4-7 \%$) under noise, revealing hidden vulnerabilities. However, closed-loop control allows agents to recover many failures, maintaining reasonable task performance. The framework highlights gaps in current evaluation practices and provides a more realistic measure of agent reliability. These findings offer a path toward developing more adaptable and deployable AI agents.

title: Architectural Patterns for Scalable Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Software Engineering Perspective
journal: 2026 International Conference on Future and Intelligent Networking (FINE)
authors: K. Savajiyani
abstract: The proliferation of large language model (LLM)-based autonomous agents has created a new class of distributed system: the multi-agent LLM network. While significant research focuses on the intelligence of individual agents, comparatively little work addresses the software architectural concerns that govern how fleets of such agents are composed, orchestrated, and scaled. This paper identifies and formalizes four recurring architectural patterns (Hierarchical Orchestration, Event-Driven Agent Mesh, Capability-Indexed Agent Registry, and Stateless Execution with Persistent Memory Offload), drawing on well-established technologies including Apache Kafka, MongoDB, AWS, Spring Boot, and Docker. All experiments were conducted exclusively on synthetically generated data using a locally hosted reference implementation on a personal development machine. No enterprise, production, or personally identifiable data was involved in this work. We analyze each pattern with respect to throughput, fault tolerance, observability, and latency trade-offs using a fully controlled synthetic workload, ensuring complete reproducibility. Our evaluation demonstrates that no single pattern dominates across all dimensions, and that composition of patterns yields the strongest results. This work provides a foundation for treating multi-agent LLM system design as a first-class software engineering discipline. Note: The four patterns operate at complementary abstraction levels coordination (Patterns 1 and 2), discovery and routing (Pattern 3), and state management (Pattern 4) and are designed for deliberate composition rather than as parallel alternatives.

title: Enhancing Autonomous Agent Accuracy Through Reflection-Based Reasoning
journal: 2026 4th International Conference on Advanced Network Technologies and Applications (APAN)
authors: L. Pang and C. Cen and J. Yu and D. Huang and X. Sun
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as reasoning engines for autonomous agents, yet their outputs remain vulnerable to inconsistency, logical errors, hallucination, and unstable multi-step inference processes. Reflection-based reasoning has emerged as an effective inference-time mechanism for improving reliability by allowing models to critique, verify, and iteratively revise their own outputs. This paper presents a controlled cross-domain empirical evaluation of three reflection strategies: Self-Refine, Reflexion, and Self-Consistency with Verification, against a baseline single-step inference approach. Experiments use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B across three core LLM evaluation datasets—GSM8K, HotpotQA, and MBPP—measuring accuracy, inference time, and token usage. Results show that reflection improves accuracy across all domains: Reflexion achieves the largest relative accuracy gains, with improvements of +8% on GSM8K, +4% on HotpotQA, and +6% on MBPP. However, all reflection methods introduce increased computational cost, especially in code generation tasks. The findings indicate that reflection is a context-dependent strategy whose practical value depends on task structure, accuracy requirements, and available computational resource constraints.

abstract: This paper presents a collaborative multi-agent framework for autonomous code generation and debugging. These systems integrate tool enabled LLMs to access external APIs, execute tests, and iteratively refine code, addressing the limitations of single models in complex software tasks. Benchmarks reveal that while LLMs excel in pattern matching, multi-agent collaboration significantly improves performance in repo-level programming and bug resolution. Emerging approaches featuring graph-based coordination and self-debugging loops demonstrate the potential for self-evolving agent networks. However, challenges in scalability and robustness necessitate hybrid human-AI workflows. This collaborative framework represents a paradigm shift from single-model synthesis towards autonomous, end-to-end software development.

title: Leveraging Agentic Coding for Interactive Education in Electrical Engineering
journal: 2026 27th International Conference on Computational Problems of Electrical Engineering (CPEE)
authors: B. Sawicki and T. Les and T. Grzywacz
abstract: Large language models enable the automated synthesis of interactive educational software beyond conversational tutoring. This paper presents an authoring methodology using agentic coding (an autonomous, tool-augmented workflow based on the Reason-and-Act (ReAct) paradigm) to generate standalone, browser-based simulation modules for electrical engineering curricula. It was applied across three undergraduate courses, using three distinct agentic development environments: a transient commutation simulator for second-order RLC circuits (circuit theory), an eddy-current induction laboratory (electromagnetism), and an interactive benchmark of iterative linear solvers (numerical methods). We formalize a pipeline built on (1) strict decoupling of pedagogical specification from implementation, (2) formal mathematical notation constraints, (3) singlepass holistic generation to prevent context window degradation, (4) human-in-the-loop validation gates, and (5) prompt-level regeneration rather than conversational code patching. Recurring failure modes: notation drift, context saturation, feature creep, and physically invalid simulations ("vibe physics"); are analyzed together with their mitigations, and an independent analytical audit of two generated modules is reported. Modules are synthesized in 5–10 minutes over 3–5 specification iterations, shifting instructor effort from manual programming to requirements engineering and domain verification.

title: RGD: Multi-LLM Based Agent Debugger via Refinement and Generation Guidance
journal: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Agents (ICA)
authors: H. Jin and Z. Sun and H. Chen
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown incredible potential in code generation tasks, and recent research in prompt engineering have enhanced LLMs’ understanding of textual information. However, ensuring the accuracy of generated code often requires extensive testing and validation by programmers. While LLMs can typically generate code based on task descriptions, their accuracy remains limited, especially for complex tasks that require a deeper understanding of both the problem statement and the code generation process. This limitation is primarily due to the LLMs’ need to simultaneously comprehend text and generate syntactically and semantically correct code, without having the capability to automatically refine the code. In real-world software development, programmers seldom produce flawless code on their first attempt. Instead, iterative feedback and debugging are heavily leveraged to refine the programs. Inspired by this process, we introduce a novel architecture of LLM-based agents for code generation and automatic debugging: Refinement and Guidance Debugging (RGD). The RGD framework is a multi-LLM-based agent debugger that leverages three distinct LLM agents-Guide Agent, Debug Agent, and Feedback Agent. RGD decomposes the code generation task into multiple steps, ensuring a clearer workflow and enabling iterative code refinement based on self-reflection and feedback. Experimental results demonstrate that RGD exhibits remarkable code generation capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a $9.8 \%$ improvement on the HumanEval dataset and a $\mathbf{1 6. 2 \%}$ improvement on the MBPP dataset compared to the state-of-theart approaches and traditional direct prompting approaches. We highlight the effectiveness of the RGD framework in enhancing LLMs’ ability to generate and refine code autonomously.

title: Rethinking LLM Evaluation: A Comprehensive Survey, Taxonomy, and the Evaluation Trilemma
journal: 2026 IEEE World AI IoT Congress (AIIoT)
authors: V. Tiwari and R. Othman and O. Suaifan and D. Wang
abstract: The evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) from specialized systems to versatile, essential platforms has created an urgent demand for thorough and effective evaluation methods. Nonetheless, current assessment methods continue to be disjointed, depending on diverse benchmarks and metrics that do not adequately reflect actual performance, reasoning accuracy, and alignment with safety standards. This document offers a cohesive and structured examination of LLM assessment via a hierarchical classification that encompasses capability dimensions, evaluation methods, and metric formulation. Expanding upon this framework, we perform an extensive meta-analysis of 312 benchmarks released since 2020, uncovering ongoing disparities in capability coverage, methodological compromises, and a notable performance gap in tasks involving autonomous agents. We present the evaluation trilemma to elucidate these limitations, highlighting the fundamental conflict between authenticity, scalability, and contamination resistance in existing evaluation frameworks. We conduct a deeper examination of innovative evaluation methods that integrate learning-based and hybrid strategies to tackle these challenges. The results underscore the necessity for cohesive and flexible assessment frameworks that accurately represent practical implementation scenarios and establish a systematic basis for progressing the evaluation of future LLMs.

title: A Multi-Agent LLM Environment for Software Design and Refactoring: A Conceptual Framework
journal: SoutheastCon 2025
authors: V. Rajendran and D. Besiahgari and S. C. Patil and M. Chandrashekaraiah and V. Challagulla
abstract: Modern software systems demand continuous evolution to maintain performance, scalability, and security. Traditional single-agent AI-driven code refactoring approaches are often limited in addressing the multi-faceted constraints (e.g., performance, security, maintainability) that emerge during complex software design tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel Multi-Agent Large Language Model (LLM) Environment for automated software design and refactoring. Our conceptual framework comprises specialized LLM “experts,” each trained or fine-tuned on a different aspect of software engineering (performance optimization, security hardening, UI/UX, maintainability). These agents collaborate in a cooperative or competitive fashion-using coordination protocols akin to consensus or auction mechanisms-to synthesize design insights and refactoring recommendations. We present formal definitions of agent interactions (including mathematical notation for termination conditions), a sequence diagram demonstrating agent collaboration, a complexity analysis of the coordination mechanism, and an expanded reference list. Preliminary experimental design is outlined to demonstrate how multi-agent interactions may resolve conflicting design goals more effectively than a single-agent approach. Our aim is to provide a roadmap for integrating multi-agent LLMs into the software development lifecycle, thereby improving development efficiency, reducing technical debt, and enhancing software quality.

title: RTLFixer: Automatically Fixing RTL Syntax Errors with Large Language Models
journal: 2024 61st ACM/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC)

abstract: This paper presents RTLFixer, a novel framework enabling automatic syntax errors fixing for Verilog code with Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite LLM’s promising capabilities, our analysis indicates that approximately 55% of errors in LLM-generated Verilog are syntax-related, leading to compilation failures. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel debugging framework that employs Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and ReAct prompting, enabling LLMs to act as autonomous agents in interactively debugging the code with feedback. This framework demonstrates exceptional proficiency in resolving syntax errors, successfully correcting about 98.5% of compilation errors in our debugging dataset, comprising 212 erroneous implementations derived from the VerilogEval benchmark. Our method leads to 32.3% and 10.1% increase in pass@1 success rates in the VerilogEval-Machine and VerilogEval-Human benchmarks, respectively. title: From Digital Twins to Autonomous Local Agents: Rethinking AI for Smart Water Networks
journal: IEEE Internet of Things Journal
authors: G. Restuccia and D. Garlisi and F. Giuliano and A. Pagano and I. Tinnirello
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled water distribution networks (WDNs) increasingly rely on digital twins (DTs) to support monitoring and decision-making, yet most DTs remain passive dashboards. Deploying artificial intelligence (AI) within these critical infrastructures requires efficient, autonomous solutions at the edge, where operational constraints and data sovereignty concerns limit the suitability of proprietary cloud-based services that expose sensitive telemetry beyond internal boundaries. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) impose significant computational and energy demands, making lightweight and locally executable agentic pipelines essential for practical deployment under edge constraints. This work introduces a modular multiagent framework that provides an on-demand DT service capable of executing complex “what-if” hydraulic analyses directly at the network edge. The system employs an autonomous agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline that enables locally deployed LLMs to interpret user intents, retrieve domain-specific context, generate simulation workflows, and self-correct execution errors without human intervention. This multiagent design yields robust and trustworthy behavior even under strict resource constraints. Beyond introducing the framework, this work systematically assesses its trustworthiness and feasibility for edge deployment by benchmarking task reliability, hardware requirements, and energy efficiency. Evaluation across a representative benchmark of WDNs shows that the proposed agentic approach improves full-task success rates by up to 30%–40% over 0-shot prompting and reduces execution failures by more than 50%. Moreover, 4-bit quantized local models deliver performance competitive with proprietary cloud solutions while lowering peak VRAM usage and energy consumption by over 60%. These results demonstrate the viability of effective, efficient, and trustworthy AI agents operating entirely on edge hardware to securely and autonomously enable advanced IoT infrastructure services.

title: BuilDroid: A Self-Correcting LLM Agent for Automated Android Builds
journal: 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

abstract: The continuous evolution of the Android ecosystem has led to a highly dynamic and fragmented development environment. This constant churn makes building Android projects, especially from open-source repositories, a notoriously difficult task. Developers and researchers encounter a daunting build barrier due to the rapid configuration drift, which results in a cascade of errors. These errors include version incompatibilities, missing dependencies, and inconsistent project configurations, hindering reproducibility and maintainability.To address these issues, we present BuilDroid, an LLM-based agent that automates the build process of Android projects. Operating within a self-contained, isolated environment, BuilDroid runs an iterative, self-correcting loop. Through this operation, BuilDroid captures errors and autonomously resolves them, either through predefined heuristics or by leveraging the reasoning capabilities of its underlying LLM.Across 245 open-source Android projects, BuilDroid effectively resolves complex and evolving build errors, achieving a build success rate of 90.2%, surpassing existing solutions by a margin of over 30.2 percentage points. title: Human-Machine Teaming and Team Effectiveness in AI Tools for Software Engineering

authors: I. Rauf and H. Sharp and T. Lopez and M. Wermelinger
abstract: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to support software engineering (SE), shifting the role of AI tools for SE (AI4SE) towards team members rather than simply tools. Human-machine teaming (HMT) views humans and machines as members of a team. This approach may be useful in AI4SE but HMT and team effectiveness have received little attention in the software engineering community. Objective: To unpick whether and how HMT and team effectiveness have been applied in AI4SE, and to identify recommendations. Method: A mapping study approach identifies 21 papers on developercentred AI4SE. Each one is analysed to identify its use of HMT, its focus regarding AI-developer interaction, and any elements of team effectiveness. Results: Different aspects of AI-developer interaction have been considered but only one paper explicitly uses the HMT concept. Some elements of team effectiveness are considered, but others are not addressed at all, and several studies do not consider any. Conclusion: Researchers are encouraged to consider HMT as a framework for AI4SE, to leverage research in all-human teams, adaptive UX and developer motivation to inform tool design, and reduce reliance on human monitoring.

title: Coding Agents in the Wild: Failure Modes and Rejection Patterns of AI-Generated Pull Requests
journal: IEEE Access
authors: M. Hindi and Y. Mahmood and L. Mohammed and S. Bouktif and M. Mediani
abstract: Autonomous coding agents increasingly submit pull requests (PRs) to real software repositories, making it important to evaluate their behavior under actual review, testing, and governance workflows rather than only through synthetic benchmarks. This paper investigates how agent-generated pull request (APR) rejection evolves over time, which visible failure modes are most evident among commented rejected APRs (RAPRs), and how these findings inform more effective coding-agent deployment and design. We follow a three-phase methodology. First, we construct an APR cohort from the AIDev-POP subset of the AIDev dataset, covering 12,433 APRs from 1,495 popular repositories and five coding agents. Second, we develop a socio-technical taxonomy of rejection reasons and validate a large language model (LLM)-based classifier on a manually labeled ground-truth subset of commented RAPRs, achieving 85.5% accuracy in identifying the main bucket reasons of the rejection. Third, we model temporal rejection patterns and conduct stratified analyses across agents, deployment settings, and reviewer types. Observational results show a significant decline in APR rejection odds over time after accounting for differences in change size, documentation and test updates, and agent type. This decline is not limited to a single agent in particular. Empirical results show that documentation co-changes are associated with lower rejection odds, whereas test-touch and patch size provide weaker differentiation. Most RAPRs are silent, with 84.2% closed without inline reviewer feedback. Among commented RAPRs, functional failures are the dominant visible rejection pattern, especially specification mismatch and logic defects. Overall, APR outcomes reflect interactions among agent behavior, repository guardrails, and developer practices. We translate these findings into evidence-informed design principles and advocate reflexive coding agent as a new design pattern that emphasizes context acquisition, local validation, and closer alignment with repository expectations. Our replication package is available at: https://github.com/mahdhindi/coding-agents-wild

title: Can LLMs Resolve Dependencies? A Benchmark for Semantic-Versioning Constraint Reasoning and Dependency Resolution
journal: 2026 8th International Conference on Electronics and Communication, Network and Computer Technology (ECNCT)
authors: Z. Wang and H. Zhang and J. Hou and S. Zheng
abstract: A coding agent that installs packages and untangles version conflicts is implicitly reasoning about semantic-versioning constraints and dependency resolution. Whether current language models can actually do this has not been measured, and that is the gap we address. DepResolve-Bench is a programmatically generated benchmark scored by a deterministic oracle that needs no human labels. We trust the oracle: it agrees with the production node-semver on 2250 sampled cases and, for resolution, with exhaustive search on 3000 instances. The benchmark has two tasks: deciding whether a version satisfies a range over the full npm grammar (Task A), and resolving a multi-package dependency graph or proving it unsatisfiable (Task B), with instance size as a difficulty knob. Five frontier and lightweight API models agree. They have nearly mastered the atomic rules, with Task A macro accuracy spanning 0.92 to 1.00, yet they cannot reliably put those rules together. On resolution the best model reaches 0.91 and the weakest 0.29, and every model degrades as the graphs grow, the strongest falling to 0.82 on the largest instances. A missed satisfiable instance almost always breaks a transitive constraint; on an unsatisfiable one, weaker models invent a resolution anyway (GPT-4o-mini for 44 of 80 such cases, the strongest model for one). How much we let a model reason matters more than which model it is: capped at 200 output tokens every model sits near 0.1, and accuracy climbs as the budget grows. We release the generators, oracle, and item banks; the results argue for keeping a real resolver in the loop rather than handing dependency management to a language model.

title: Benchmarking AI Coding Assistants: Prompt Sensitivity in Gemini 2.5 Flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B

authors: I. Kaur and R. Kumar Nath and K. S. Buchireddy and A. Tiwary and A. Shakya
abstract: Talk shapes code now, not strict rules typed by hand. A small twist in how words are said can flip everything around. Swap just one term, watch the direction jump elsewhere - little things pull hard on results. Old-school checks stay fixed, repeat the same steps every time. Real conversations? They zigzag, backtrack, spin off suddenly. Meaning grows unevenly, never quite where you expect. Programs must keep up, step by step, no matter how wild the flow. One peek under the hood revealed word flow shapes outcomes across two models - Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash, Meta’s LLaMA-3.3-70B. When speed played a role, Gemini pulled ahead each time. Success crowned most attempts, landing close to 96 percent done. Though LLaMA clocked past twenty seconds, Gemini frequently answered before ten elapsed. Trouble hit LLaMA in almost three out of ten tries, usually since replies ended mid-sentence. Still standing when pressure built, even if both began at the same pace. Close to a hundred trials unfolded - divided by how questions were framed and what kind of tasks were given. Clearer context gave a small boost - but differences didn’t close. One gliding ahead while the second stumbled again and again. Speed changes expose tiny delays that quietly add up. A shift becomes clear when studying these numbers. Closed tools resist the flow of real work rather than joining it. Once systems such as GPT-4 or Claude face deeper trials, perception could flip. What appears as one kind of code here may emerge unrecognizable there. Breaking major jobs into pieces leads to outcomes distant from rushed solo attempts.

title: ASIC-Agent: An Autonomous Multi-Agent System for ASIC Design with Benchmark Evaluation
journal: 2025 IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD)
authors: A. Allam and Y. Mansour and M. Shalan
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in Register Transfer Level (RTL) design, enabling high-quality code generation from natural language descriptions. However, LLMs alone face significant limitations in real-world hardware design workflows, including the inability to execute code, lack of debugging capabilities, and absence of long-term memory. To address these challenges, we present ASIC-Agent, an autonomous system designed specifically for digital ASIC design tasks. ASIC-Agent enhances base LLMs with a multi-agent architecture incorporating specialized subagents for RTL generation, verification, OpenLane hardening, and Caravel chip integration, all operating within a comprehensive sandbox environment with access to essential hardware design tools. The system leverages a vector database containing documentation, API references, error knowledge, and curated insights from the open-source silicon community. To evaluate ASIC-Agent’s performance, we introduce ASIC-Agent-Bench, the first benchmark specifically designed to assess agentic systems in hardware design tasks. We evaluate ASIC-Agent with various base LLMs, providing quantitative comparisons and qualitative insights into agent behavior across different design scenarios. Our results demonstrate that ASIC-Agent, when powered by Claude 4 Sonnet, successfully automates a broad range of ASIC design tasks spanning varying levels of complexity, showing the potential of significantly accelerating the ASIC design workflow. title: AutoGPT Devloop: An Autonomous AI Development Framework for End-to-End Software Generation, Execution, and Self-Repair

abstract: We present the Autonomous AI Development Framework (AADF), a self-developing agent that converts high-level goals into functioning software through iterative planning, code generation, execution, and self-repair. AADF integrates (i) task decomposition, (ii) a semantic code memory (vector database), (iii) virtualized environment management, and (iv) automated file/version control to achieve autonomy across the software lifecycle. Using a Design Science Research approach, we evaluate AADF on a suite of $15 \text{GUI} /$ web tasks spanning five difficulty levels (3 trials each; 45 trials). The framework achieves 100% success on Levels 1-2 and Level 4, with partial degradations on tasks dependent on external API credentials or large NLP resources (Level 3: $67 {\%} / 33 {\%}$ on two tasks; Level 5: 67% on one task). Overall, AADF completes $41 / 45$ trials $(91.1 {\%})$ without manual code editing, demonstrating reliable self-repair for dependency conflicts and missing imports, and reducing human effort on environment setup, boilerplate, and repetitive file operations. We discuss error taxonomies (credentials, heavyweight downloads, concurrency), autonomy-speed trade-offs, and actionable design guidelines for safe deployment in practice.

title: RepoTransBench: A Real-World Multilingual Benchmark for Repository-Level Code Translation
journal: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
authors: Y. Wang and Y. Wang and S. Wang and D. Guo and J. Chen and J. Grundy and X. Liu and Y. Ma and M. Mao and H. Zhang and Z. Zheng
abstract: Repository-level code translation refers to translating an entire code repository from one programming language to another while preserving the functionality of the source repository. Many benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate the performance of such code translators. However, previous benchmarks mostly provide fine-grained samples, focusing at either code snippet, function, or file-level code translation. Such benchmarks do not accurately reflect real-world demands, where entire repositories often need to be translated, involving longer code length and more complex functionalities. To address this gap, we propose a new benchmark, named RepoTransBench, which is a real-world multilingual repository-level code translation benchmark featuring 1,897 real-world repository samples across 13 language pairs with automatically executable test suites. Besides, we introduce RepoTransAgent, a general agent framework to perform repository-level code translation. We evaluate both our benchmark’s challenges and agent’s effectiveness using several methods and backbone LLMs, revealing that repository-level translation remains challenging, where the best-performing method achieves only a 32.8% success rate. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that translation difficulty varies significantly by language pair direction, with dynamic-to-static language translation being much more challenging than the reverse direction (achieving below 10% vs. static-to-dynamic at 45-63%). Finally, we conduct a detailed error analysis and highlight current LLMs’ deficiencies in repository-level code translation, which could provide a reference for further improvements. We provide the code and data at https://github.com/DeepSoftwareAnalytics/RepoTransBench.
